idiom_name: explicit FIFO queue + reified event records + one drain point
implementation_notes: Language-neutral form: reify each request or notification as a small record carrying the data the receiver will need later, append it to a FIFO queue (fixed ring buffer when the pending window is bounded, growable deque otherwise) and return to the sender immediately. One owner drains the queue at a defined point - once per simulation tick, in the event loop, or on a dedicated worker thread - handling items directly or routing them to registered listeners. Decide the overload policy up front (block, drop oldest, drop newest, coalesce duplicates, back-pressure), make the queue thread-safe only if it really spans threads, and end the drain deterministically with a stop flag or close token.
code_sketch:
post(event):                 # reify + enqueue, return immediately
    queue.push_back(event)

drain_once_per_tick():       # the only place that processes
    while not queue.empty():
        handle(queue.pop_front())
pitfalls: Letting the sender call the handler directly 'just this once' recreates the timing coupling the queue removes.
Events that reference live objects or world state instead of copying the data they need break when processed later — use generation-counters or liveness checks at handler entry.
An unbounded queue with no overload policy turns a slow receiver into a memory leak that grows until the process dies.

Dangling references: an event references an entity (e.g., a GameObject) that is destroyed before drain. The handler dereferences a dead pointer. Mitigation: stable entity IDs with generation counters, liveness checks, or self-contained event payloads.

Priority inversion in multi-threaded queues: a low-priority thread holds the queue mutex while a high-priority thread blocks trying to enqueue. Use priority-inheritance mutexes (e.g., FreeRTOS xSemaphoreCreateMutex, not binary semaphores).
Memory allocation inside the event path: malloc/free in real-time or ISR contexts is non-deterministic. Pre-allocate from a fixed-block pool sized to the worst-case in-flight count.

Re-entrancy feedback loops: handler A posts an event that triggers handler B which posts back to A — cycles spin silently without stack overflow. Rule: avoid sending events from inside a handler, or use a two-pass drain that captures the pending batch before dispatch.
Ignoring queue-full returns: a dropped event due to a full-bounded-queue can mean a missed state transition. Count and surface overflow events; treat them as errors, not benign back-pressure.

Wrong move: assume post() dispatches synchronously as its javadoc promises -> posting from inside a handler is queued behind the current dispatch, so a handler that blocks on work the deferred event would release deadlocks (Guava EventBus re-entrant thread-local queue) -> instead make posting from handlers explicit: defer to the next drain pass or use a separate side-channel queue.

Wrong move: drain with 'while not empty: pop' while handlers feed the same queue -> a self-sustaining event cycle livelocks the loop and starves every other per-frame job -> instead capture the pending batch at drain start (swap buffers / two-phase drain) and defer mid-drain posts to the next cycle.

Wrong move: treat every enqueue as a distinct observable occurrence -> coalescing queues fire one callback for many posts (libuv uv_async_send) or collapse duplicates (Qt paint-event compression), so per-event counting or per-event side effects silently go missing -> instead never use the queue as a counter; carry an explicit sequence number or count in the payload.
